Content:
A dilation of scale factor [MATH: k] with the center at the origin is a linear transformation that multiplies the standard basis vectors by [MATH: k.] It is represented by the matrix
[MATH: [k|0; 0|k]]

Content:
For example, let [MATH: [2|0; 0|2]] be the matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}.] This transformation is a dilation of scale factor [MATH: 2.]

Content:
To visualize the dilation [MATH: \mathbf{T},] consider the standard basis [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] of the Euclidean plane [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the unit square [MATH: \mathrm{R}] spanned by the vectors, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/5b0f6bfa4dae673897b259120e1c15ca]

Content:
We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: T,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: i^{′}|= Ti = [2|0; 0|2][1; 0] = [2; 0] = 2i,; j^{′}|= Tj = [2|0; 0|2][0; 1] = [0; 2] = 2j.]

Content:
The transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] multiplies vectors [MATH: \mathbf{i}] and [MATH: \mathbf{j}] by [MATH: 2.] The resulting vectors span a larger region, shown below.

sections.normalized_html: A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a dilation. Given that [MATH: [24; 16]] and [MATH: [6; 4]] what is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]
sections.readable_text: A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a dilation. Given that [MATH: [24; 16]] and [MATH: [6; 4]] what is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can write [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] as follows:

[MATH: T(v)|= [6; 4]; = (1)/(4) ⋅ [24; 16]; = (1)/(4)v]

Since we have [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{v},] we conclude that the linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] is a dilation with scale factor [MATH: k = \dfrac{1}{4}.]

Remember that the matrix representing a dilation of scale factor [MATH: k] is given by [MATH: [k|0; 0|k]]

Therefore, the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is [MATH: [(1)/(4)|0; 0|(1)/(4)]]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

[MATH: [k|0; 0|k]]

Content:
For example, let [MATH: [2|0; 0|2]] be the matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}.] This transformation is a dilation of scale factor [MATH: 2.]

Content:

The transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] multiplies vectors [MATH: \mathbf{i}] and [MATH: \mathbf{j}] by [MATH: 2.] The resulting vectors span a larger region, shown below.

Item 2 — Example: Finding the Standard Matrix of a Dilation Given a Vector and its Image

A linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}] represents a dilation. Given that [MATH: [24; 16]] and [MATH: [6; 4]] what is the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We can write [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] as follows:

[MATH: T(v)|= [6; 4]; = (1)/(4) ⋅ [24; 16]; = (1)/(4)v]

Since we have [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) = \dfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{v},] we conclude that the linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf T] is a dilation with scale factor [MATH: k = \dfrac{1}{4}.]

Remember that the matrix representing a dilation of scale factor [MATH: k] is given by
[MATH: [k|0; 0|k]]

Therefore, the standard matrix of [MATH: \mathbf{T}] is
[MATH: [(1)/(4)|0; 0|(1)/(4)]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Consider the standard basis [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] of the Euclidean plane [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as depicted below.

We can find the images of [MATH: \{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}] under [MATH: T,] as follows:

[MATH: i^{′}|= T(i) = [1|0; 0|− 1][1; 0] = [1; 0] = i; j^{′}|= T(j) = [1|0; 0|− 1][0; 1] = [0; − 1] = − j]

Then, we obtain the following image:
